elements.quote: In this systematic review, a search of PubMed, CINAHL, PsycINFO, EMBASE, and Web of Science (January 2000-May 2021) was performed, and quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods studies were included.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly states that the work is “this systematic review.”

elements.quote: To improve older patients' physical activity (PA) behavior, it is important to identify facilitators and barriers to enhancing PA in older patients ( ≥ 65 years) during hospitalization from the perspectives of patients, caregivers, and healthcare professionals (HCPs).
elements.reason: The abstract provides an explicit aim/objective describing what the review intends to identify.
The abstract does not specify explicit main inclusion and exclusion criteria.

elements.quote: Methods: In this systematic review, a search of PubMed, CINAHL, PsycINFO, EMBASE, and Web of Science (January 2000-May 2021) was performed,
elements.reason: The abstract identifies the information sources (databases) and provides a search time range, but it does not state when each source was last searched (as an explicit last-search date).

elements.quote: The methodological quality of included studies was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the method/tool used to assess methodological quality (risk of bias/quality appraisal).

elements.quote: Identified facilitators and barriers were categorized using the social ecological model at the intrapersonal, interpersonal, and institutional levels.
elements.reason: The abstract describes how results were presented/synthesized (categorization using the social ecological model).

elements.quote: Results: The 48 included articles identified 230 facilitators and 342 barriers.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies (48 articles) but does not report the total number of participants.

elements.quote: The main facilitators at the intrapersonal level included: knowledge, awareness, and attitudes; interpersonal level: social support, including encouragement and interdisciplinary collaboration; and institutional level: stimulating physical environment, patient activities and schedules, and PA protocols. The main barriers at the intrapersonal level included: physical health status, having lines or drains, patients' fear, and HCPs' safety concerns; interpersonal level: patient-HCP relation and HCPs' unclear roles; and institutional level: lack of space and resources, including time and equipment.
elements.reason: The abstract presents results for main outcomes (facilitators/barriers and their themes), but it does not include the number of included studies and participants for each outcome.
There is no indication in the abstract that a meta-analysis was conducted; therefore, no summary estimate or confidence/credible interval is applicable.
The abstract does not report any group comparisons with a direction of effect; thus this conditional item does not apply.
The abstract does not briefly summarize important limitations of the included evidence (e.g., risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision).

elements.quote: Conclusion: The PA behavior of older adults during hospitalization is multidimensional. Our overview highlights facilitators and barriers on multilevel scale (intrapersonal, interpersonal, and institutional levels) that guides patients, caregivers, HCPs, and researchers in future clinical practice, and intervention development and implementation.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a general interpretation and discusses implications for future practice and intervention development.
No primary source of funding is reported in the provided abstract evidence.
The provided abstract evidence does not state the register name and registration number.

elements.quote: To be included in this review, studies had to explore facilitators and/or barriers to PA in older patients during hospitalization. Studies were included if: 1) they were published between January 1, 2000, and May 29, 2021; 2) they were written in English, German, or Dutch; 3) they used a quantitative, qualitative, or mixed-methods study design; and 4) the study population consisted of patients aged ≥ 65 years (baseline mean age of 65 years or older), caregivers, or HCPs.
elements.reason: Eligibility is specified for study question/context (older patients during hospitalization), study designs (quantitative/qualitative/mixed-methods), and study population. However, follow-up requirements are not described, and the evidence does not fully specify all framework components for eligibility (e.g., follow-up).

elements.quote: The initial search of the databases yielded 19,060 records. After removing duplicates, a total of 12,690 articles were screened on title and abstract, of which 12,590 did not meet the inclusion criteria. Of the 100 articles for which the full text was read, another 52 did not meet the inclusion criteria.
elements.reason: Reports the number of records identified (19,060), removed before screening (duplicates removed), screened (12,690), and excluded after initial screening (12,590), plus full-text read and excluded (52).

No numbers are reported for reports sought but not retrieved, assessed for eligibility, or excluded with primary reasons (beyond full-text exclusion counts without explicit breakdown corresponding to PRISMA 2020 subcategories).

elements.quote: The 48 articles included in the review comprised 18 qualitative, 19 quantitative, and 11 mixed-methods studies (Additional file 5).

elements.quote: The methodological quality scores of the included quantitative studies ranged from no score to a maximum score of 5 (Additional file 6). elements.quote: One researcher (FD) extracted data from the selected full-text studies.
elements.reason: The evidence describes data extraction from full-text studies, but does not report the source of study-level data in cases where multiple data sources were used.

elements.quote: Subsequently, the overall quality scores of each study were used to group studies into two categories: high (MMAT score 4 or 5) and low (MMAT score 0-3) quality.
elements.reason: The evidence indicates that scores were calculated and used for grouping studies, but it does not identify which results/outcome data were computed or estimated versus directly reported for study outcomes.

elements.quote: The approach considered the study's quality (defined by MMAT scores), study design, the number of articles, and finding consistency, to classify the evidence as strong, moderate, limited, conflicting, or insufficient [36] (Table 1).
elements.reason: The review describes how it assessed contributing studies’ quality using MMAT scores (used to categorize evidence levels), but it does not explicitly summarise characteristics and risk of bias “for each synthesis,” nor does it clearly label this as “risk of bias.”

The retrieved evidence does not identify which specific studies contributed to each synthesis (e.g., which studies were included per synthesis), only general counts/descriptions of included studies and overarching synthesis methods.

elements.quote: Our best evidence synthesis results ranged from insufficient to moderate levels of evidence, of which results classified with limited and moderate levels of evidence were reported in the sections below.
elements.reason: The evidence reports outcomes of a best evidence synthesis (levels of evidence for barriers/facilitators), but it does not demonstrate that results of all pre-specified and additional statistical syntheses are fully reported.
No meta-analysis summary estimates with precision (e.g., CI/credible interval) are reported in the retrieved evidence.
No measures of statistical heterogeneity (e.g., I²/τ²) for any meta-analysis are reported in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: The best evidence synthesis suggested moderate evidence for three barriers: patients' unwillingness or refusal to move, patients having symptoms, and having lines or drains (Additional file 8). elements.reason: The evidence provides synthesized (best evidence synthesis) classifications for specific facilitators/barriers, but it does not include relevant statistics/quantitative measures or a fully question-consistent interpretation beyond the evidence level labeling.

The retrieved evidence includes a PRISMA flow figure and guidance/quality tables, but does not display sensitivity-analysis results in forest plots.
